common_name: Flordasun Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; a very low chilling requirement lets this cultivar bloom and set fruit reliably in mild Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Released by the University of Florida breeding program in the mid-1960s, Flordasun quickly replaced the earlier 'Flordawon' as the leading early peach for central Florida because its fruit held up better to handling and shipping. It bears medium-large, yellow-skinned, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit that ripens early in the season on a very low chill requirement. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil, prune to an open vase in the first years, and thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once they size up. Fertilize lightly in spring and again after harvest to support repeat cropping in warm-winter climates.

common_name: Flordagold Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; needs only around 325-350 chill hours, so it fruits dependably through mild Gulf South winters.

directions: Developed by the University of Florida low-chill peach breeding program, Flordagold stood out in multi-location trials for its unusually large, firm fruit and attractive skin color, earning top firmness ratings among the cultivars tested. It ripens early to mid-season with semi-freestone flesh that handles well for backyard and local-market growers. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, train to an open-vase form, and thin young fruit to roughly 6-8 inches apart so remaining fruit size up well. A light spring feeding and a second application after harvest keep trees vigorous for the next crop.

common_name: Flordabelle Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Semi-Clingstone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; a roughly 200-hour chilling requirement suits it to the mildest Gulf South winters.

directions: Bred at the University of Florida from a 1960 cross involving 'Flordawon', Flordabelle was selected as an improved, brighter-skinned successor to the earlier 'Newbelle' peach, with a golden-yellow ground color under a red blush. It is a large, semi-clingstone peach that ripens early to mid-season, among the first fresh peaches available in warm-winter gardens. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, prune to an open center, and thin crowded fruit clusters so the remaining peaches reach full size. Because it is self-fertile, a single tree will set a crop, though a second early-blooming peach nearby can improve pollination.

common_name: Flordagem Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; its low chilling requirement is similar to 'Flordagold' but it ripens about a week earlier.

directions: A sibling release from the same University of Florida program that produced 'Flordagold', Flordagem shares that cultivar's attractive yellow ground color and firm texture but matures roughly a week sooner and carries noticeably less skin fuzz. This makes it a useful option for Gulf South growers who want to spread their peach harvest window earlier in the season. Plant in full sun on well-drained ground, prune to an open-vase shape, and thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once they reach marble size. Light feeding in spring and after harvest supports consistent annual cropping.

common_name: Flordawon Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Historic Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; among the lowest-chill peaches ever named, it blooms and ripens very early even in mild winters.

directions: Named by the University of Florida breeding program in 1961, Flordawon was one of the first low-chill peaches recommended for trial in central Florida, valued for its very low chilling requirement and late-April to early-May harvest. Its fruit proved too soft for commercial shipping, so plantings stayed small and it was soon overtaken by sturdier releases such as 'Flordasun', but it remains historically important as a parent of later cultivars including 'Flordabelle'. Home growers in the mildest Gulf South locations can still use it for an exceptionally early homegrown peach. Plant in full sun with good drainage, keep fruit thinned, and pick promptly at ripeness since the soft flesh does not hold well once mature.

common_name: UFBlaze Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Non-Melting-Flesh Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; a roughly 300-chill-hour requirement suits it to Gulf South winters.

directions: Bred by Wayne B. Sherman at the University of Florida and released by Florida Foundation Seed Producers from a cross with a non-melting nectarine selection and 'UFGold', UFBlaze produces large, early-ripening clingstone fruit with vivid red skin over a yellow-orange background and firm yellow flesh that resists bruising during handling. Vigorous, heavy-cropping trees ripen in early May at Gainesville, roughly a week to ten days after 'UFGold'. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, prune to an open center, and thin fruit while still marble-sized to improve final size. The firm, non-melting texture makes this a good choice for growers who want peaches that travel or store a bit better than soft-fleshed types.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP14,898 (Wayne B. Sherman)

common_name: UFO Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Donut-Shaped Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; a chilling requirement of around 250 hours lets it bloom and ripen very early in warm-winter gardens.

directions: Bred by Wayne B. Sherman at the University of Florida, UFO is a flattened, saucer- or donut-shaped (peento-type) peach with firm, yellow, non-melting flesh and showy pink spring blossoms on a large, vigorous tree. Its early bloom and roughly 250-hour chilling need made it one of the first non-melting, peento-shaped peaches described for subtropical, low-chill conditions in the United States. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, prune to an open-vase form in early years, and thin the flattened fruit to about 6 inches apart to encourage good size. The firm flesh holds up well to handling, a useful trait for home orchardists sharing or selling surplus fruit.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP13,352 (Wayne B. Sherman)

common_name: UF2000 Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Non-Melting-Flesh Clingstone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while fully dormant; it needs roughly 300 chill hours, well within what mild Gulf South winters reliably supply.

directions: Bred at the University of Florida by Wayne B. Sherman, UF2000 is a heavy-cropping, moderately large clingstone peach with highly colored skin and good eating quality for a non-melting type. It ripens mid-to-late season at Gainesville, roughly two weeks ahead of 'UFGold', and its firm flesh holds its tree-ripe flavor and texture for about ten days without softening, which is handy for home growers who cannot harvest every tree daily. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, train young trees to an open-vase shape, and thin fruit while small to improve final size. Light fertilization in spring and after harvest keeps annual production consistent.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP12,019 (Wayne B. Sherman)
